question.text: In the 20th century, this Southern Hemisphere country built a nearly 3500-mile fence to keep dingos, a type of wild dog that lives in this country's outback, out of its more populated southeast.
question.clue: In this country, the murder of James Scobie at Ballarat led to an insurrection of gold miners in the Eureka Rebellion.

swap.leadin: Descendents of convicts known as "currency lads" carried out raids on feral horses called brumbies in the bush and this region.
swap.text: Name this region where jackaroos established "cattle empires" around stations. The disastrous Emu War occurred in this rural region of central Australia.
swap.clue: An overland telegraph line through this region was scouted by Robert Burke and William Wills but was eventually built through Alice Springs.

question.leadin: This colony was founded by the First Fleet on January 26, 1788, and its first governor was Arthur Phillip.
question.text: Name this colony which originated around Port Jackson. Lachlan Macquarie was the final governor of this territory.
question.clue: The Tenterfield Oration, calling for states to unify for purposes of defense, was given in this state, which was also the landing spot for Arthur Phillip and the First Fleet.

swap.text: The "history wars" began after the Bringing Them Home report was released on these people. This term refers to Australian Aborigines taken from their families as children by the Australian government.
swap.clue: An official 2007 apology to these people and their descendants was made by then-Prime Minister Kevin Rudd.

question.leadin: Answer the following about the only successful armed uprising in Australian history.
question.text: Major George Johnston invaded Government House and placed Bligh under arrest in this capital city of New South Wales.
question.clue: This city is the largest to be served by the Snowy Mountains Hydroelectric Scheme, whose construction caused its country to ease pro-white immigration policies.

swap.leadin: Malcolm Fraser came to power after a 1975 constitutional crisis in Australia.
swap.text: Fraser succeeded Gough (goff) Whitlam, the leader of this political party, which shares its name, but not its American-style spelling, with one of the two main parties in the U.K.
swap.clue: This political party passed important social reforms under leaders like Bob Hawke and Gough Whitlam.

question.leadin: As Treasurer of Australia, this man oversaw the creation of the Australian Dollar and later ended the pegging of the currency to the British pound.
question.text: Name this Prime Minister who more famously went missing while swimming at Cheviot Beach in 1967. Ironically, a swimming pool in Melbourne was named in his honor.
question.clue: This prime minister declared that he was "all the way with LBJ" in showing his country's support for the Vietnam War.

swap.leadin: Major G.P.W. Meredith once said that if the military had a division with the bullet-carrying capacity of the opposing side in this conflict, they could face any army in the world.
swap.text: Name this conflict in which an army, despite having machine guns, lost to a bunch of flightless birds.
swap.clue: One side in this war was targeted because they kept creating gaps in rabbit fences.

question.leadin: Following this event, Lachlan Macquarie was appointed governor of a certain colony.
question.text: Name this rebellion, caused by James MacArthur's importation of the titular alcoholic drink.
question.clue: Others associated with this event included John Blaxland and Richard Atkins, and it saw resistance along the after the storming of the Government House.

swap.leadin: During World War II, the US 1st Marine Division adopted this ballad by Banjo Paterson as their official march.
swap.text: Name this song, which "the Band Played" in an Eric Bogle song memorializing the Gallipoli campaign. It is considered Australia's "unofficial national anthem."
swap.clue: While at an outback station, Banjo Paterson wrote this "unofficial Australian anthem" which describes a "jolly swagman camped by a billabong." This song's title refers to the motion of a "tucker bag" containing a "jumbuck."

question.leadin: The Stolen Generations were children of these people who were forcibly taken from their families and resettled into white communities.
question.text: Name these indigenous inhabitants of Australia.
question.clue: Many of these people were taken from their families and integrated into white culture, becoming the Stolen Generation.

swap.leadin: Identify some things about the geography of Australia.
swap.text: This tallest mountain in Australia takes its name from a similar peak in Poland, which is named after a Polish hero of the American Revolutionary War.

question.leadin: A 1920 act titled "Protection of" [this word] bans using this word for commercial purposes, except when referring to its namesake oatmeal coconut "biscuits."
question.text: What word names an April 25th holiday that commemorates the amphibious landing of an Army Corps made up of forces from two Commonwealth countries, as well as the cove where they landed?
question.clue: Their most notable action is remembered in the song titled "And the Band Played" a certain nationalist folk tune, was supported by the French from Kum Kale, and was advocated by Winston Churchill.

swap.leadin: Critics derided this man as "British to his bootstraps" due to his extreme monarchism.
swap.text: Name this Liberal politician who also tried to ingratiate himself with ordinary citizens by delivering the 'Forgotten People' Speech. He was succeeded by Harold Holt.
swap.clue: This World War II-era Prime Minister of Australia served for a record 18 years. After an electoral defeat, he formed the Liberal Party to provide conservative opposition to the Labor Party.

question.text: Menzies built credit among the middle class by calling them by this name, which titles a notable 1942 speech he made emphasizing his connections to ordinary people.

swap.leadin: These people circulated Yirrkala Bark Petitions to raise concerns about the sale of land to bauxite-mining companies and set up a "tent embassy" in Canberra to oppose it.
swap.text: Name these people whose "Stolen Generations" of children were forcibly assimilated into Australian society.
swap.answerHtml: Indigenous Australians [or Aboriginal Australians; accept Yolŋu; accept Torres Strait Islanders]

question.leadin: A famous cartoon of this event depicts the Governor of the territory in which it took place cowering under his bed.
question.text: Name this uprising, led by George Macarthur. Macarthur was angered by, among other things, a lien against one of his ships for abetting an escaped convict and Major George Johnston.
question.clue: This rebellion took place after the arrest of John Macarthur, a lieutenant of the New South Wales Corp. It was named for the nickname of the New South Wales Corp, which had to do with a product the Corp traded.

swap.text: While charting the coast of Arnhem Land, this explorer encountered a Makassan trepang fleet led by chief Pobasso. This Royal Navy officer is credited as the first person to use the name Australia.
swap.clue: This explorer was a member of William Bligh's Second Breadfruit Voyage that successfully brought the crop to the Caribbean.

question.text: Later, New Zealand and Australia laid out their post-WWII military and political goals in the Canberra Pact, signed by this Australian prime minister. Frank Forde finished this prime minister's term after his death in office.
question.clue: This prime minister of Australia during World War Two, a member of the Labour Party, defended the policy by declaring the country "the home of the British race" in a 1942 speech.

swap.leadin: Matthew Brady, not to be confused with the American photographer, was known as a "gentleman" one of these people and was an enemy of Governor George Arthur. FTPE.
swap.text: Identify this group of outlaws that included Ned Kelly.
swap.clue: "Bolters" like John "Black" Caesar made up the first generation of this profession, whose later practitioners included Mary Ann Bugg and her lover, Captain Thunderbolt.
